claim: Cerebellar mossy fiber boutons (cMFBs) are characterized by fast vesicle replenishment mediating high-frequency signaling.
source: Here, we investigated the Ca2+-sensitivity of these steps at mossy fiber synapses in the rodent cerebellum, which are characterized by fast vesicle replenishment mediating high-frequency signaling.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established characteristic of the synapse being studied.

claim: The basal free Ca2+ concentration (<200 nM) critically controls action potential-evoked release at cerebellar mossy fiber synapses.
source: We found that the basal free Ca2+ concentration (<200 nM) critically controls action potential-evoked release, indicating a high-affinity Ca2+ sensor for vesicle priming.
evidence: This finding is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: A high-affinity Ca2+ sensor mediates vesicle priming at cerebellar mossy fiber synapses.
source: We found that the basal free Ca2+ concentration (<200 nM) critically controls action potential-evoked release, indicating a high-affinity Ca2+ sensor for vesicle priming.
evidence: This interpretation is stated in the abstract based on the observed Ca2+ dependence of action potential-evoked release.

claim: The relationship between release rate and intracellular Ca2+ concentration is surprisingly shallow and non-saturating up to 50 μM at cerebellar mossy fiber synapses.
source: Ca2+ uncaging experiments revealed a surprisingly shallow and non-saturating relationship between release rate and intracellular Ca2+ concentration up to 50 μM.
evidence: This finding is explicitly stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figures 2-4.

claim: The rate of vesicle replenishment during sustained elevated intracellular Ca2+ concentration exhibits little Ca2+-dependence at cerebellar mossy fiber synapses.
source: The rate of vesicle replenishment during sustained elevated intracellular Ca2+ concentration exhibited little Ca2+-dependence.
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 5.

claim: Quantitative mechanistic release schemes with five Ca2+ binding steps incorporating rapid vesicle replenishment via parallel or sequential vesicle pools can explain the experimental data from cerebellar mossy fiber synapses.
source: Finally, quantitative mechanistic release schemes with five Ca2+ binding steps incorporating rapid vesicle replenishment via parallel or sequential vesicle pools could explain our data.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the abstract and supported by modeling results in Figure 6.

claim: Co-existing high- and low-affinity Ca2+ sensors mediate priming, fusion, and replenishment of synaptic vesicles at cerebellar mossy fiber synapses.
source: We thus show that co-existing high- and low-affinity Ca2+ sensors mediate priming, fusion, and replenishment of synaptic vesicles at a high-fidelity synapse.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract, synthesizing the findings from the study.

claim: The presynaptic vesicle cycle includes priming of neurotransmitter-filled vesicles, fusion of primed vesicles, and replenishment of new vesicles after fusion.
source: Neurotransmitter release is mediated by the presynaptic vesicle cycle (Südhof, 2004) including (1) the priming of neurotransmitter-filled vesicles, (2) the fusion of primed vesicles, and (3) the replenishment of new vesicles after fusion.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to Südhof, 2004.

claim: The basal free intracellular Ca2+ concentration is approximately 50 nM.
source: While the basal free intracellular Ca2+ concentration is ~50 nM, thousandfold higher local microdomains of Ca2+ build and decay very fast around the Ca2+ channels (Simon and Llinás, 1985; Yamada and Zucker, 1992).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Simon and Llinás, 1985 and Yamada and Zucker, 1992.

claim: Local microdomains of Ca2+ around Ca2+ channels can reach concentrations thousandfold higher than basal levels and build and decay very fast.
source: While the basal free intracellular Ca2+ concentration is ~50 nM, thousandfold higher local microdomains of Ca2+ build and decay very fast around the Ca2+ channels (Simon and Llinás, 1985; Yamada and Zucker, 1992).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Simon and Llinás, 1985 and Yamada and Zucker, 1992.

claim: Ca2+ uncaging allows for homogenous elevation of Ca2+ concentration throughout the whole presynaptic compartment via UV-photolysis of caged Ca2+ compounds.
source: Ca2+ uncaging circumvented this problem by allowing for the homogenous elevation of Ca2+ concentration throughout the whole presynaptic compartment via UV-photolysis of caged Ca2+ compounds (Kaplan and Ellis-Davies, 1988) and thus the direct measurement of the Ca2+-concentration immediately relevant for vesicle fusion (reviewed by Neher, 1998; Kochubey et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Kaplan and Ellis-Davies, 1988; Neher, 1998; and Kochubey et al., 2011.

claim: First experiments with Ca2+ uncaging at retinal bipolar cells of goldfish found a very low sensitivity of the release sensors with a half saturation at approximately 100 μM Ca2+ concentration.
source: First experiments with Ca2+ uncaging at retinal bipolar cells of goldfish found a very low sensitivity of the release sensors with a half saturation at ∼100 μM Ca2+ concentration and a fourth to fifth power relationship between Ca2+ concentration and neurotransmitter release (Heidelberger et al., 1994), similar to previous estimates at the squid giant synapse (Adler et al., 1991; Llinás et al., 1992).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Heidelberger et al., 1994; Adler et al., 1991; and Llinás et al., 1992.

claim: Analysis of the calyx of Held at a young pre-hearing age found a much higher affinity with significant release below 5 µM intracellular Ca2+ concentration and a steep dose-response curve.
source: For example, analysis of a central excitatory synapse, the calyx of Held (Forsythe, 1994) at a young pre-hearing age, found a much higher affinity with significant release below 5 µM intracellular Ca2+ concentration and a steep dose-response curve (Bollmann et al., 2000; Lou et al., 2005; Schneggenburger and Neher, 2000; Sun et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Forsythe, 1994; Bollmann et al., 2000; Lou et al., 2005; Schneggenburger and Neher, 2000; and Sun et al., 2007.

claim: The calyx of Held shows a developmental decrease in the Ca2+-sensitivity of vesicle fusion.
source: Further analysis of the calyx of Held during neuronal development comparing the Ca2+-sensitivity of the release sensors at the age of P9 to P12-P15 (Kochubey et al., 2009) and P9 to P16-P19 (Wang et al., 2008) showed a developmental decrease in the Ca2+-sensitivity of vesicle fusion.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Kochubey et al., 2009 and Wang et al., 2008.

claim: Hippocampal mossy fiber boutons of rats (P18–30) show a high Ca2+-sensitivity of vesicle fusion with a steep dose-response curve.
source: Studies at two other central synapses, the hippocampal mossy fiber boutons of rats (P18–30; Fukaya et al., 2021) and the boutons of cerebellar basket cells of mice (P11-16; Sakaba, 2008), also described a high Ca2+-sensitivity of vesicle fusion with a steep dose-response curve.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to Fukaya et al., 2021.

claim: The boutons of cerebellar basket cells of mice (P11-16) show a high Ca2+-sensitivity of vesicle fusion with a steep dose-response curve.
source: Studies at two other central synapses, the hippocampal mossy fiber boutons of rats (P18–30; Fukaya et al., 2021) and the boutons of cerebellar basket cells of mice (P11-16; Sakaba, 2008), also described a high Ca2+-sensitivity of vesicle fusion with a steep dose-response curve.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to Sakaba, 2008.

claim: The dose-response curve of sensory neurons of the rod photoreceptors is more shallow than that of the calyx of Held.
source: In contrast, the dose-response curve of sensory neurons of the rod photoreceptors was more shallow (Duncan et al., 2010; Thoreson et al., 2004) and vesicle fusion below 7 µM Ca2+ concentration was absent at the cochlear inner hair cells (Beutner et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Duncan et al., 2010 and Thoreson et al., 2004.

claim: Vesicle fusion below 7 µM Ca2+ concentration is absent at the cochlear inner hair cells.
source: In contrast, the dose-response curve of sensory neurons of the rod photoreceptors was more shallow (Duncan et al., 2010; Thoreson et al., 2004) and vesicle fusion below 7 µM Ca2+ concentration was absent at the cochlear inner hair cells (Beutner et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to Beutner et al., 2001.

claim: Vesicle priming refers to the molecular and positional preparation of vesicles for fusion near Ca2+ channels.
source: We refer to vesicle priming as the molecular and positional preparation of vesicles for fusion near Ca2+ channels (Neher and Sakaba, 2008).
evidence: This definition is stated in the introduction with a citation to Neher and Sakaba, 2008.

claim: Molecular priming is the functional correlate of vesicle docking.
source: Molecular priming has recently been shown to be the functional correlate of vesicle docking (Imig et al., 2014; Maus et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Imig et al., 2014 and Maus et al., 2020.

claim: Vesicle replenishment refers to the delivery of new vesicles during sustained activity.
source: Vesicle replenishment refers to the delivery of new vesicles during sustained activity.
evidence: This definition is stated in the introduction.

claim: The size of the pool of fast-releasing vesicles linearly depends on the intracellular Ca2+ concentration at the calyx of Held synapse.
source: First, the size of the pool of fast-releasing vesicles linearly depends on the intracellular Ca2+ concentration at the calyx of Held synapse (Hosoi et al., 2007; see also Awatramani et al., 2005; Wang and Kaczmarek, 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Hosoi et al., 2007; Awatramani et al., 2005; and Wang and Kaczmarek, 1998.

claim: The sustained component of release linearly depends on the intracellular Ca2+ concentration at cerebellar basket cell synapses.
source: Second, the sustained component of release, presumably reflecting vesicle replenishment, linearly depends on the intracellular Ca2+ concentration at cerebellar basket cell synapses (Sakaba, 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to Sakaba, 2008.

claim: The number of docked vesicles is rapidly and reversibly regulated depending on the resting Ca2+ levels and neuronal activity at hippocampal neurons.
source: Third, the number of docked vesicles assessed by electron microscopic techniques is rapidly and reversibly regulated depending on the resting Ca2+ levels and neuronal activity at hippocampal neurons (Chang et al., 2018; Imig et al., 2020; Kusick et al., 2020; Vandael et al., 2020; Vevea et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Chang et al., 2018; Imig et al., 2020; Kusick et al., 2020; Vandael et al., 2020; and Vevea et al., 2021.

claim: The occupancy of the docking sites increases upon elevating extracellular Ca2+ levels at cerebellar synapses.
source: Fourth, the occupancy of the docking sites increases upon elevating extracellular Ca2+ levels at cerebellar synapses (Blanchard et al., 2020; Malagon et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Blanchard et al., 2020 and Malagon et al., 2020.

claim: Previous studies at cerebellar mossy fiber synapses could explain release during trains of action potentials or prolonged depolarizations with Ca2+-independent vesicle priming and replenishment.
source: In contrast, previous studies at cerebellar mossy fiber synapses could explain release during trains of action potentials or prolonged depolarizations with Ca2+-independent vesicle priming and replenishment (Hallermann et al., 2010; Ritzau-Jost et al., 2014; Ritzau-Jost et al., 2018; Saviane and Silver, 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Hallermann et al., 2010; Ritzau-Jost et al., 2014; Ritzau-Jost et al., 2018; and Saviane and Silver, 2006.

claim: The cerebellar mossy fiber bouton conveys high-frequency sensory information to the cerebellar cortex and relies on extremely fast vesicle replenishment.
source: The cerebellar mossy fiber bouton (cMFB) conveys high-frequency sensory information to the cerebellar cortex and relies on extremely fast vesicle replenishment (Miki et al., 2020; Ritzau-Jost et al., 2014; Saviane and Silver, 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Miki et al., 2020; Ritzau-Jost et al., 2014; and Saviane and Silver, 2006.

claim: The free Ca2+ concentration in the presynaptic intracellular solution was 28 ± 3 nM for the low basal Ca2+ condition.
source: Two-photon quantitative Ca2+ imaging with the dual-indicator method using Fluo-5F as the Ca2+ indicator (Delvendahl et al., 2015; Sabatini et al., 2002) revealed the free Ca2+ concentration of the presynaptic intracellular solution to be 28 ± 3 and 183 ± 8 nM, for the low and high basal Ca2+ conditions (n = 4 and 4), respectively (Figure 1A).
evidence: This measurement is reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 1A, using two-photon Ca2+ imaging.

claim: The free Ca2+ concentration in the presynaptic intracellular solution was 183 ± 8 nM for the high basal Ca2+ condition.
source: Two-photon quantitative Ca2+ imaging with the dual-indicator method using Fluo-5F as the Ca2+ indicator (Delvendahl et al., 2015; Sabatini et al., 2002) revealed the free Ca2+ concentration of the presynaptic intracellular solution to be 28 ± 3 and 183 ± 8 nM, for the low and high basal Ca2+ conditions (n = 4 and 4), respectively (Figure 1A).
evidence: This measurement is reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 1A, using two-photon Ca2+ imaging.

claim: The EPSC amplitude was 39 ± 8 pA for the low basal Ca2+ condition.
source: On average, the EPSC amplitudes were 39 ± 8 and 117 ± 28 pA for the low and high basal Ca2+ conditions, respectively (n = 8 and 8; PMann-Whitney = 0.028; Figure 1D).
evidence: This measurement is reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The EPSC amplitude was 117 ± 28 pA for the high basal Ca2+ condition.
source: On average, the EPSC amplitudes were 39 ± 8 and 117 ± 28 pA for the low and high basal Ca2+ conditions, respectively (n = 8 and 8; PMann-Whitney = 0.028; Figure 1D).
evidence: This measurement is reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: There is an almost threefold increase in the EPSC amplitude when elevating the resting Ca2+ concentration in the presynaptic terminals from 30 to 180 nM.
source: We found an almost threefold increase in the EPSC amplitude when elevating the resting Ca2+ concentration in the presynaptic terminals from 30 to 180 nM.
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section based on the data in Figure 1.

claim: The frequency of miniature currents had a tendency to increase with elevated basal Ca2+ concentration (median 1.1 and 3.5 Hz for the low and high basal Ca2+ conditions, respectively).
source: Interestingly, the frequency of miniature currents in-between the current injections used to elicit action potentials had a tendency to increase with elevated basal Ca2+ concentration (median 1.1 and 3.5 Hz for the low and high basal Ca2+ conditions, respectively, n = 8 and 8; PMann-Whitney = 0.13; data not shown).
evidence: This observation is reported in the Results section with statistical analysis.

claim: The EPSC rise and decay kinetics were not significantly different between low and high basal Ca2+ conditions.
source: The EPSC rise and decay kinetics were not significantly different (Figure 1D).
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: No significant differences were observed in the action potential waveform including amplitude and half duration between low and high basal Ca2+ conditions.
source: No significant differences were observed in the action potential waveform including amplitude and half duration (Figure 1D) indicating that the altered synaptic strength was not caused by changes in the shape of the presynaptic action potential.
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Moderate changes in the presynaptic basal Ca2+ concentration can alter synaptic strength up to threefold.
source: These data indicate that moderate changes in the presynaptic basal Ca2+ concentration can alter synaptic strength up to threefold.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the Results section based on the data in Figure 1.

claim: Prominent vesicle fusion occurs at Ca2+ concentrations below 5 µM at cerebellar mossy fiber boutons.
source: At low Ca2+ concentrations (<5 µM), a significant amount of neurotransmitter release could be measured, which is consistent with previous reports from central synapses (Bollmann et al., 2000; Fukaya et al., 2021; Sakaba, 2008; Schneggenburger and Neher, 2000).
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section with citations to previous studies.

claim: The presynaptic release rates increased with increasing post-flash Ca2+ concentration and no saturation in the release rate occurred in the dose-response curve.
source: The presynaptic release rates increased with increasing post-flash Ca2+ concentration and no saturation in the release rate occurred in the dose-response curve (Figure 3D).
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Fitting a Hill equation to the deconvolution data resulted in a best-fit KD >50 µM and a Hill coefficient of 1.6.
source: Fitting a Hill equation to the deconvolution data resulted in a best-fit KD >50 µM and a Hill coefficient of 1.6 (Figure 3D).
evidence: This result is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Two independent measures of synaptic release (presynaptic capacitance measurements and postsynaptic deconvolution analysis) indicate a non-saturating shallow dose-response curve up to approximately 50 µM.
source: Therefore, two independent measures of synaptic release (presynaptic capacitance measurements and postsynaptic deconvolution analysis) indicate a non-saturating shallow dose-response curve up to ~50 µM.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the Results section based on data from Figures 2 and 3.

claim: The KD of OGB-5N is approximately 30 µM.
source: We estimated a KD of OGB-5N of ~30 µM being at the lower range of previous estimates ranging from 20 to 180 µM (Delvendahl et al., 2015; DiGregorio and Vergara, 1997; Neef et al., 2018), arguing against an erroneously high KD of the Ca2+ indicator as a cause for the non-saturation.
evidence: This measurement is reported in the Results section with citations to previous studies and is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Approximately 40% of all recordings were classified as bi-exponential (38 out of 80 capacitance measurements and 17 out of 59 deconvolution experiments).
source: Consistent with a visual impression, this standardized procedure resulted in the classification of ~40% of all recordings as bi-exponential (38 out of 80 capacitance measurements and 17 out of 59 deconvolution experiments; Figure 4C D).
evidence: This result is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4C-D.

claim: The release rate of the fast component of the merged capacitance and deconvolution data showed no signs of saturation.
source: The release rate of the fast component (1/τ1) of the merged capacitance and deconvolution data showed no signs of saturation consistent with our previous analyses of each data set separately.
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section based on data in Figure 4C.

claim: Fitting a Hill equation to the merged data indicated a KD >50 μM and a Hill coefficient of 1.6.
source: Fitting a Hill equation to the merged data indicated a KD >50 μM and a Hill coefficient of 1.6 (Figure 4C).
evidence: This result is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The release rate of the slow component was on average more than 10 times smaller than the fast component.
source: The release rate of the slow component (1/τ2; if existing) was on average more than 10 times smaller (black symbols, Figure 4C).
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: There are at least two distinct kinetic steps contributing to release within the first 10 ms at cerebellar mossy fiber boutons.
source: These data indicate that there are at least two distinct kinetic steps contributing to release within the first 10 ms.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the Results section based on the bi-exponential fits shown in Figure 4.

claim: The slope of the sustained component of release is, if anything, weakly dependent on the intracellular Ca2+ concentration in the range of 1–50 µM.
source: These data indicate that the slope of the sustained component of release is, if anything, weakly dependent on the intracellular Ca2+ concentration in the range of 1–50 µM, consistent with previously observed Ca2+-independent vesicle replenishment as assessed by depolarizing cMFBs to 0 mV in the absence or presence of intracellular EGTA (Ritzau-Jost et al., 2014).
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the Results section based on data in Figure 5 and cited previous work.

claim: The simulations predict little overshoot of Ca2+ following UV illumination with short laser pulses compared to the Ca2+ concentration measured by the Ca2+ indicator.
source: In contrast to previous results, which predicted a significant overshoot of Ca2+ following UV illumination with short laser pulses (Bollmann et al., 2000), our simulations predict little overshoot compared to the Ca2+ concentration measured by the Ca2+ indicator (Figure 6B).
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6B, with a citation to Bollmann et al., 2000.

claim: The calculations predict an almost step-like increase in the free Ca2+ concentration with a 10–90% rise time below 50 µs.
source: The calculations predict an almost step-like increase in the free Ca2+ concentration with a 10–90% rise time below 50 µs.
evidence: This result is stated in the Results section based on simulations.

claim: Model 1 with a single pool of vesicles with two Ca2+ binding steps could not reproduce the synaptic delay.
source: However, adjusting the free parameters did not allow reproducing the synaptic delay (Figure 6E).
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Model 3 reproduced the data as good as model 2; however, the non-saturation up to 50 µM could be reproduced somewhat better in model 3.
source: Model 3 reproduced the data as good as model 2; however, the non-saturation up to 50 µM could be reproduced somewhat better in model 3.
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section based on modeling results in Figure 6.

claim: Models 2 and 3 both replicated the observed shallow dose-response curve despite the presence of five Ca2+ binding steps.
source: Interestingly, models 2 and 3 both replicated the observed shallow dose-response curve despite the presence of five Ca2+ binding steps.
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section based on modeling results in Figure 6.

claim: Established models with five Ca2+-steps incorporating fast vesicle replenishment via sequential or parallel vesicle pools can replicate the experimental data fairly well.
source: These results indicate that established models with five Ca2+-steps incorporating fast vesicle replenishment via sequential or parallel vesicle pools can replicate our data fairly well.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the Results section based on modeling results in Figure 6.

claim: The peak EPSC amplitude of postsynaptic current was significantly larger with high compared to low pre-flash Ca2+ concentration (38 ± 10 and 91 ± 16 pA, n = 18 and 13, respectively, PMann-Whitney = 0.001).
source: The peak EPSC amplitude of postsynaptic current was significantly larger with high compared to low pre-flash Ca2+ concentration (38 ± 10 and 91 ± 16 pA, n = 18 and 13, respectively, PMann-Whitney = 0.001; Figure 7A and C).
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7A and C.

claim: The amplitude of the fast component of release as measured from deconvolution analysis was larger with high compared to low pre-flash Ca2+ (18 ± 5 and 49 ± 10, n = 18 and 13, respectively, PMann-Whitney = 0.005).
source: Correspondingly, the amplitude of the fast component of release as measured from deconvolution analysis was larger with high compared to low pre-flash Ca2+ (18 ± 5 and 49 ± 10, n = 18 and 13, respectively, PMann-Whitney = 0.005; Figure 7C).
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The kinetics of vesicle fusion were not significantly different for low and high pre-flash Ca2+ conditions (0.15 ± 0.04 and 0.12 ± 0.03 ms−1, n = 18 and 13, respectively, PMann-Whitney = 0.74).
source: However, the kinetics of vesicle fusion, measured as the inverse of the time constant of the fast component of release, were not significantly different for both conditions (0.15 ± 0.04 and 0.12 ± 0.03 ms−1 for the low and high pre-flash Ca2+ conditions, n = 18 and 13, respectively, PMann-Whitney = 0.74; Figure 7C).
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The number of release-ready vesicles were increased upon elevating the basal Ca2+ concentration but the fusion kinetics were unaltered.
source: These data indicate that the number of release-ready vesicles were increased upon elevating the basal Ca2+ concentration but the fusion kinetics were unaltered.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the Results section based on data in Figure 7.

claim: The release schemes 2 and 3 describe all the experimental data and represent the only release scheme explaining the priming, fusion, and replenishment of vesicles at a mature excitatory synapse in the CNS at physiological temperature.
source: Thus, the release schemes 2 and 3 describe all our experimental data and therefore represent to our knowledge the only release scheme explaining the priming, fusion, and replenishment of vesicles at a mature excitatory synapse in the CNS at physiological temperature.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the Results section based on the modeling results.

claim: The Ca2+-sensitivity of vesicle fusion seems to be synapse-specific.
source: The Ca2+-sensitivity of vesicle fusion seems to be synapse-specific.
evidence: This statement is made in the Discussion section based on the review of literature.

claim: The shallow and non-saturating dose-response curve is the consequence of rapid replenishment of vesicles that still exhibit a lower Ca2+-affinity compared to fully recovered vesicles.
source: Our data therefore indicate that the shallow and non-saturating dose-response curve is the consequence of rapid replenishment of vesicles that still exhibit a lower Ca2+-affinity compared to fully recovered vesicles.
evidence: This interpretation is stated in the Discussion section based on the experimental and modeling results.

claim: A lowering in the Ca2+-affinity of the vesicle fusion sensor has been observed at the calyx of Held with Ca2+ uncaging following vesicle depletion.
source: Consistent with this interpretation, a lowering in the Ca2+-affinity of the vesicle fusion sensor has been observed at the calyx of Held with Ca2+ uncaging following vesicle depletion (Müller et al., 2010; Wadel et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to Müller et al., 2010 and Wadel et al., 2007.

claim: The cerebellar mossy fiber bouton has a much faster rate of vesicle replenishment compared with the calyx of Held synapse.
source: These newly replenished vesicles might contribute particularly to the dose-response curve at the cMFB because the cMFB has a much faster rate of vesicle replenishment compared with the calyx of Held synapse (Miki et al., 2020) providing a possible explanation why the here-reported dose-response curve differs from previous results at the calyx of Held.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation to Miki et al., 2020.

claim: Cerebellar mossy fiber boutons have functional similarities with ribbon-type synapses because the vesicle mobility in cMFBs is comparable to ribbon-type synapses.
source: Furthermore, cMFBs seem to have functional similarities with ribbon-type synapses because it has recently been shown that the vesicle mobility in cMFBs is comparable to ribbon-type synapses (Rothman et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation to Rothman et al., 2016.

claim: The hallmark of ribbon-type synapses is their rapid vesicle replenishment.
source: The hallmark of ribbon-type synapses is their rapid vesicle replenishment (Lenzi and von Gersdorff, 2001; Matthews, 2000) and indeed more shallow dose-response curves were obtained at the ribbon photoreceptors and inner hair cell synapses (Duncan et al., 2010; Heil and Neubauer, 2010; Johnson et al., 2010; Thoreson et al., 2004, but see Beutner et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to Lenzi and von Gersdorff, 2001; Matthews, 2000; Duncan et al., 2010; Heil and Neubauer, 2010; Johnson et al., 2010; Thoreson et al., 2004; and Beutner et al., 2001.

claim: The newly replenished vesicles might be molecularly immature and resemble vesicles that have only a near-linear remaining Ca2+ sensor when the fast Ca2+ sensor synaptotagmin II is lacking.
source: The newly replenished vesicles might be molecularly immature and resemble vesicles that have only a near-linear remaining Ca2+ sensor when the fast Ca2+ sensor synaptotagmin II is lacking (Kochubey and Schneggenburger, 2011).
evidence: This speculation is stated in the Discussion section with a citation to Kochubey and Schneggenburger, 2011.

claim: The Ca2+-dependence of vesicle priming and replenishment at cMFBs was analyzed more indirectly with the Ca2+ chelator EGTA in previous reports.
source: In previous reports, the Ca2+-dependence of vesicle priming and replenishment at cMFBs was analyzed more indirectly with the Ca2+ chelator EGTA (Ritzau-Jost et al., 2014; Ritzau-Jost et al., 2018) and the obtained results could be explained by Ca2+-dependent models but surprisingly also by Ca2+-independent models (Hallermann et al., 2010; Ritzau-Jost et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to Ritzau-Jost et al., 2014; Ritzau-Jost et al., 2018; and Hallermann et al., 2010.

claim: The recovery from depression is independent of the Ca2+/calmodulin/Munc13 pathway at cMFBs.
source: Furthermore, the analysis of molecular pathways showed that the recovery from depression is independent of the Ca2+/calmodulin/Munc13 pathway at cMFBs (Ritzau-Jost et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation to Ritzau-Jost et al., 2018.

claim: Some priming steps are mediated by Ca2+-dependent mechanisms, which do not involve the Ca2+/calmodulin/Munc13 pathway at cMFBs.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that some priming steps are mediated by Ca2+-dependent mechanisms, which do not involve the Ca2+/calmodulin/Munc13 pathway.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the Discussion section based on the current and previous findings.

claim: A potential candidate for a Ca2+-dependent mechanism of priming is the interaction of diacylgylcerol/phospholipase C or Ca2+/phospholipids with Munc13s.
source: A potential candidate for such a Ca2+-dependent mechanism are the interaction of diacylgylcerol/phospholipase C or Ca2+/phospholipids with Munc13s (Lee et al., 2013; Lou et al., 2008; Rhee et al., 2002; Shin et al., 2010).
evidence: This speculation is stated in the Discussion section with citations to Lee et al., 2013; Lou et al., 2008; Rhee et al., 2002; and Shin et al., 2010.

claim: Another candidate for a high-affinity Ca2+ sensor is Synaptotagmin 7.
source: Another candidate for a high-affinity Ca2+ sensor is Synaptotamin 7 (see below).
evidence: This speculation is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: Synaptic vesicles that fuse upon single action potentials and weak uncaging stimuli might represent the superprimed vesicles with a particular high release probability.
source: Synaptic vesicles that fuse upon single action potentials (Figure 1) and weak uncaging stimuli (post-flash Ca2+ concentration of ~3 µM; Figure 7) are particularly fusogenic and thus might represent the superprimed vesicles with a particular high release probability (Hanse and Gustafsson, 2001; Ishiyama et al., 2014; Kusch et al., 2018; Lee et al., 2013; Schlüter et al., 2006; Taschenberger et al., 2016) suggesting that the process of superpriming is Ca2+-dependent.
evidence: This interpretation is stated in the Discussion section with citations to Hanse and Gustafsson, 2001; Ishiyama et al., 2014; Kusch et al., 2018; Lee et al., 2013; Schlüter et al., 2006; and Taschenberger et al., 2016.

claim: The process of superpriming is Ca2+-dependent.
source: Synaptic vesicles that fuse upon single action potentials (Figure 1) and weak uncaging stimuli (post-flash Ca2+ concentration of ~3 µM; Figure 7) are particularly fusogenic and thus might represent the superprimed vesicles with a particular high release probability (Hanse and Gustafsson, 2001; Ishiyama et al., 2014; Kusch et al., 2018; Lee et al., 2013; Schlüter et al., 2006; Taschenberger et al., 2016) suggesting that the process of superpriming is Ca2+-dependent.
evidence: This is inferred in the Discussion section based on the experimental findings and cited literature.

claim: The data are consistent with a proposed rapid, dynamic, and Ca2+-dependent equilibrium between primed and superprimed vesicles.
source: It would be furthermore consistent with a proposed rapid, dynamic, and Ca2+-dependent equilibrium between primed and superprimed vesicles (Neher and Brose, 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation to Neher and Brose, 2018.

claim: The strong dependence of the action potential-evoked release on basal Ca2+ supports the critical effect of residual Ca2+ on synaptic strength.
source: The strong dependence of the action potential-evoked release on basal Ca2+ (Figure 1) supports the critical effect of residual Ca2+ on synaptic strength.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the Discussion section based on the data in Figure 1.

claim: The mechanistic analysis indicates that the number of release-ready vesicles rather than the vesicular release probability is regulated by residual Ca2+.
source: Our mechanistic analysis (particularly Figure 7) indicates that the number of release-ready vesicles rather than the vesicular release probability is regulated by residual Ca2+.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the Discussion section based on the data in Figure 7.

claim: The high-affinity Ca2+ sensor Synaptotagmin-7 could be a sensor for the changes in basal Ca2+ levels and mediate the three-fold increase in synaptic strength.
source: The high-affinity Ca2+ sensor Synaptotagmin-7 (Sugita et al., 2002) could be a sensor for the changes in basal Ca2+ levels and mediate the here-reported three-fold increase in synaptic strength (Figures 1 and 7).
evidence: This speculation is stated in the Discussion section with a citation to Sugita et al., 2002.

claim: Synaptotagmin-7 has been shown to mediate vesicle recruitment, asynchronous release, and synaptic facilitation.
source: Synaptotagmin-7 has been shown to mediate vesicle recruitment (Liu et al., 2014), asynchronous release (Luo and Südhof, 2017), and synaptic facilitation (Chen et al., 2017; Jackman et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to Liu et al., 2014; Luo and Südhof, 2017; Chen et al., 2017; and Jackman et al., 2016.

claim: There is increasing evidence for ultra-fast Ca2+-dependent recruitment and priming.
source: Indeed, there is increasing evidence for ultra-fast Ca2+-dependent recruitment and priming (reviewed in Neher and Brose, 2018) as well as facilitation mediated by an increase in the number of release-ready vesicles rather than the vesicular release probability (Jackman et al., 2016; Kobbersmed et al., 2020; Vevea et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to Neher and Brose, 2018; Jackman et al., 2016; Kobbersmed et al., 2020; and Vevea et al., 2021.

claim: The data are consistent with the emerging view that facilitation is mediated by rapid Synaptotagmin-7/Ca2+-dependent recruitment and priming of vesicles.
source: Our data are therefore consistent with the emerging view that facilitation is mediated by rapid Synaptotagmin-7/Ca2+-dependent recruitment and priming of vesicles.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the Discussion section based on the current findings and cited literature.

claim: Synaptic fidelity has been shown to increase with age at cMFBs, neocortical synapses, and the calyx of Held.
source: Synaptic fidelity has been shown to increase with age at cMFBs (Cathala et al., 2003), neocortical synapses (Bornschein et al., 2019), and the calyx of Held (Fedchyshyn and Wang, 2005; Nakamura et al., 2015; Taschenberger and von Gersdorff, 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to Cathala et al., 2003; Bornschein et al., 2019; Fedchyshyn and Wang, 2005; Nakamura et al., 2015; and Taschenberger and von Gersdorff, 2000.

claim: During high-frequency transmission, the residual Ca2+ concentration increases up to a few µM at cMFBs.
source: During high-frequency transmission, the residual Ca2+ concentration increases up to a few µM at cMFBs (Delvendahl et al., 2015) but mature cMFBs can still sustain synchronous release (Hallermann et al., 2010; Saviane and Silver, 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to Delvendahl et al., 2015; Hallermann et al., 2010; and Saviane and Silver, 2006.

claim: Mature cMFBs can sustain synchronous release during high-frequency transmission.
source: During high-frequency transmission, the residual Ca2+ concentration increases up to a few µM at cMFBs (Delvendahl et al., 2015) but mature cMFBs can still sustain synchronous release (Hallermann et al., 2010; Saviane and Silver, 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to Hallermann et al., 2010 and Saviane and Silver, 2006.

claim: The developmental decrease in the affinity of the release sensors observed at the calyx of Held and the shallow dose-response curve at mature cMFBs could be an evolutionary adaptation of synapses to prevent the depletion of the release-ready vesicles at medium Ca2+ concentrations.
source: The developmental decrease in the affinity of the release sensors observed at the calyx of Held (Wang et al., 2008) and the here-reported shallow-dose-response curve at mature cMFBs could be an evolutionary adaptation of synapses to prevent the depletion of the release-ready vesicles at medium Ca2+ concentrations and therefore allow maintaining sustained synchronous neurotransmission with high fidelity (Matthews, 2000).
evidence: This speculation is stated in the Discussion section with citations to Wang et al., 2008 and Matthews, 2000.

claim: All recordings were performed at near-physiological temperature (36.0°C to 36.3°C).
source: All recordings were performed at near-physiological temperature by adjusting the set temperature of the TC-324B perfusion heat controller (Warner Instruments, Hamden, CT, United States) until the temperature in the center of the recording chamber with immersed objective was between 36.0°C and 36.3°C.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Acute cerebellar slices were prepared from mature P35–P42 C57BL/6 mice of either sex.
source: Acute cerebellar slices were prepared from mature P35–P42 C57BL/6 mice of either sex as previously described (Hallermann et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section with a citation to Hallermann et al., 2010.

claim: The entire pool of release-ready vesicles can fuse within less than 100 µs at cerebellar mossy fiber boutons.
source: Despite these efforts, the time constants were sometimes faster than 100 µs, representing the resolution limit of 10 kHz capacitance sampling (Figure 2E). These results indicate that the entire pool of release-ready vesicles can fuse within less than 100 µs.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the Results section based on data in Figure 2E.

claim: Fitting a Hill equation on both 5- and 10 kHz data resulted in a best-fit KD of >50 µM with a best-fit Hill coefficient, n, of 1.2.
source: Fitting a Hill equation on both 5- and 10 kHz data resulted in a best-fit KD of >50 µM with a best-fit Hill coefficient, n, of 1.2 (Figure 2F).
evidence: This result is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The delay from the onset of the UV-illumination to the onset of the rise of membrane capacitance was strongly dependent on the post-flash Ca2+ concentration.
source: The delay was strongly dependent on the post-flash Ca2+ concentration and the dose-response curve showed no signs of saturation at high Ca2+ concentrations (Figure 2G), which is consistent with the non-saturating release rates.
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The fusion kinetics of synaptic vesicles increased up to a Ca2+ concentration of 50 µM without signs of saturation, suggesting a surprisingly low apparent affinity of the fusion sensor at mature cMFBs under physiological temperature conditions (KD > 50 µM).
source: These data reveal that the fusion kinetics of synaptic vesicles increased up to a Ca2+ concentration of 50 µM without signs of saturation, suggesting a surprisingly low apparent affinity of the fusion sensor at mature cMFBs under physiological temperature conditions (KD > 50 µM).
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the Results section based on data in Figure 2.

claim: Kynurenic acid (2 mM) and cyclothiazide (100 μM) were added to the extracellular solution to prevent the saturation and desensitization of postsynaptic AMPA receptors, respectively.
source: Kynurenic acid (2 mM) and cyclothiazide (100 μM) were added to the extracellular solution in order to prevent the saturation and desensitization of postsynaptic AMPA receptors, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the experimental methods.

claim: The dose-response curve for the delay from the onset of the UV illumination to the onset of the rise of the cumulative release trace did not show signs of saturation of the release kinetics in the investigated range.
source: The dose-response curve for the delay from the onset of the UV illumination to the onset of the rise of the cumulative release trace (Equation 1) did not show signs of saturation of the release kinetics in the investigated range.
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section based on deconvolution analysis.

claim: Comparison of strong and short UV illumination (100% intensity; 0.1 ms) with weak and long UV illumination (10% intensity; 1 ms) resulted in similar post-flash concentrations but did not reveal a significant difference in the corresponding release rate.
source: Secondly, we experimentally compared strong and short UV illumination (100% intensity; 0.1 ms) with weak and long UV illumination (10% intensity; 1 ms), because a Ca2+ overshoot is expected to primarily occur with strong and short UV illumination. Comparison of these two groups of UV illumination resulted in similar post-flash concentrations but did not reveal a significant difference in the corresponding release rate indicating that undetectable Ca2+ overshoots did not affect the measured release rate (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Undetectable Ca2+ overshoots did not affect the measured release rate.
source: Comparison of these two groups of UV illumination resulted in similar post-flash concentrations but did not reveal a significant difference in the corresponding release rate indicating that undetectable Ca2+ overshoots did not affect the measured release rate (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the Results section based on data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The rate of release between 10 and 100 ms showed no obvious dependence on the post-flash Ca2+ concentration when measured by capacitance.
source: There was considerable variability in the release rate between 10 and 100 ms, which could be due to differences in bouton size and wash-out of proteins during whole-cell recordings. However, the release rate showed no obvious dependence on the post-flash Ca2+ concentration (Figure 5B).
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: A comparable dose-response curve was obtained when investigating the rate of release between 10 and 100 ms using deconvolution analysis of postsynaptic currents, with a weak but significant correlation.
source: A comparable dose-response curve was obtained when investigating the rate of release between 10 and 100 ms using deconvolution analysis of postsynaptic currents, however, with a weak but significant correlation (Figure 5C).
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The discrepancy between the current simulations and previous results predicting a significant overshoot of Ca2+ is readily described by recent improvements in the quantification of Ca2+ binding and unbinding kinetics.
source: The discrepancy is readily described by recent improvements in the quantification of Ca2+ binding and unbinding kinetics (Faas et al., 2005; Faas et al., 2007).
evidence: This explanation is stated in the Results section with citations to Faas et al., 2005 and Faas et al., 2007.

claim: At the cMFB, the coupling distance of the vesicles released by a single action potential is if anything even smaller than the previous estimate of 20 nm.
source: Therefore, at the cMFB, the coupling distance of the vesicles released by a single action potential is if anything even smaller than the previous estimate of 20 nm.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the Discussion section based on the current findings.

claim: The average connectivity ratio is 90.1 GCs per MFB.
source: Assuming a capacitance of 70 aF per vesicle (Hallermann et al., 2003), we obtained an average value of 90.1 GCs per MFB in close agreement with previous estimates using a similar approach (Ritzau-Jost et al., 2014).
evidence: This result is stated in the Materials and methods section with citations to Hallermann et al., 2003 and Ritzau-Jost et al., 2014.

claim: The connectivity ratio of 90.1 GCs per MFB is larger than previous estimates of approximately 10 and approximately 50.
source: This connectivity ratio is larger than previous estimates (∼10, Billings et al., 2014; ∼50, Jakab and Hamori, 1988) which could be due to a bias toward larger terminals, ectopic vesicle release, postsynaptic rundown, or release onto Golgi cells.
evidence: This comparison is stated in the Materials and methods section with citations to Billings et al., 2014 and Jakab and Hamori, 1988.
